questions.prompt: What false standard does Chapter 4 challenge first?
choices: That remembering everything matters more than understanding anything
That finishing pages is the same thing as learning from them
That slow reading is always better than fast reading

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter keeps separating page completion from real retention and use.
explanation.direct: Its main correction is that visible completion is not enough evidence that learning happened.

questions.prompt: Why does passive reading become a problem in this chapter?
choices: Because it can feel productive while producing weak recall and weak application
Because it proves the reader chose the wrong book
Because it only affects memory in school settings

explanation.gentle: Right. Passive reading flatters the session more than it helps the ideas stay.
explanation.direct: The danger is that time and page movement can disguise thin carryover.

questions.prompt: Which move best matches the chapter's idea of active reading?
choices: Reading without stopping so momentum never breaks
Highlighting every sentence that feels important
Pausing to restate the main idea and test recall after the page is closed

explanation.gentle: That is the chapter's practical posture: participation instead of passive exposure.
explanation.direct: Restatement and recall give the idea a better chance to become retrievable later.
explanation.competitive: Make the page leave a mark.

questions.prompt: Lena has a heavily highlighted chapter but cannot explain it without looking back. What would the chapter recommend next?
choices: Add more highlight colors so the page becomes easier to scan
Pause and restate the argument from memory before continuing
Skip recall because recognition on the page is enough

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter raises the standard from decoration to recall.
explanation.direct: Testing retrieval is stronger evidence than trusting visible page activity.
explanation.competitive: Ink is not a substitute for carryover.

questions.prompt: What stronger test of reading value does the chapter offer?
choices: Whether the idea can still be recalled, explained, or used later
Whether the reading felt fast and uninterrupted
Whether the chapter was finished in one sitting

explanation.gentle: Exactly. The chapter wants residue, not only completion.
explanation.direct: Usable retention and application are stronger evidence than page count alone.

questions.prompt: Which claim would Chapter 4 reject as a misreading?
choices: Active reading raises the odds that ideas stay usable
Review and recall can be part of reading itself
One reading trick can guarantee perfect retention for every reader

explanation.gentle: Correct. The chapter avoids miracle promises.
explanation.direct: It argues for a stronger posture, not a universal guarantee.
explanation.competitive: Better odds are the claim, not fake certainty.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat review as part of reading rather than an optional extra?
choices: Because review makes books shorter
Because review is stronger evidence that the idea entered the learner's working system
Because review replaces the need for understanding while reading

explanation.gentle: Yes. Review helps the reader see what actually stayed.
explanation.direct: The chapter folds review into reading because retrieval matters to the chapter's definition of learning.
explanation.competitive: If the idea cannot come back, the reading got too much credit.

questions.prompt: Ethan reads one section quickly and another more slowly with pauses and index-card recall. Which outcome best fits the chapter?
choices: The slower participatory session is more likely to leave usable residue the next day
The faster session is always better because page speed proves comprehension
Both sessions must produce identical carryover because the text stayed the same

explanation.gentle: The chapter would expect the more active session to leave a stronger trace.
explanation.direct: Participatory reading gives retrieval a better chance than passive speed does.
explanation.competitive: Tomorrow exposes which session actually mattered.

questions.prompt: What deeper tension does the chapter protect?
choices: Whether all books should be read at the same speed
Whether reading should always feel difficult to count as serious
How to demand better retention without turning the advice into gimmick theater

explanation.gentle: Right. The chapter wants a stronger posture without fake promises.
explanation.direct: Its anti-hype boundary keeps active reading practical instead of theatrical.
explanation.competitive: The chapter stays tough by refusing gimmick talk.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 4 prepare the reader for what comes next in the book?
choices: It finishes the methods section before mindset begins
It teaches every later memory and speed-reading technique in advance
It changes the reader's intake posture so later chapters have a better chance to stick

explanation.gentle: Yes. A better reading posture increases the yield of the chapters that follow.
explanation.direct: The chapter prepares the reader by making books active training material instead of passive inspiration.
explanation.competitive: It upgrades the intake method before the deeper system keeps building.
